sections.heading: A.2 Mitigating Posterior Collapse via Masked Reconstruction
sections.text: A.2.1 Corrupted Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) Standard VAE training optimizes the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO): ℒ ELBO = 𝔼 q ϕ ​ ( Z | X ) [ log p θ ( X | Z ) ] − β ⋅ KL ( q ϕ ( Z | X ) ∥ p ( Z ) ) , \mathcal{L}_{\text{ELBO}}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(Z|X)}[\log p_{\theta}(X|Z)]-\beta\cdot\mathrm{KL}(q_{\phi}(Z|X)\|p(Z)), (10) which balances reconstruction (first term) against regularization of the posterior q ϕ ​ ( Z | X ) q_{\phi}(Z|X) toward the prior p ⁡ ( Z ) p(Z) (second term). Under strong compression and large β \beta , this KL penalty can push q ϕ ​ ( Z | X ) q_{\phi}(Z|X) too close to p ⁡ ( Z ) p(Z) , causing posterior collapse : q ϕ ​ ( Z | X ) ≈ p ⁡ ( Z ) q_{\phi}(Z|X)\approx p(Z) . At this point, Z Z carries no information about X X , and the decoder effectively becomes an unconditional model p θ ​ ( X ) p_{\theta}(X) , leading to poor reconstructions. MacTok takes a different approach by training on masked images. Let X ~ \tilde{X} be the masked image after applying a stochastic masking operation C m ​ ( X ~ | X ) C_{m}(\tilde{X}|X) with ratio m m . The encoder sees only X ~ \tilde{X} , but the decoder must still reconstruct the full image X X . This gives us the corrupted ELBO : ℒ corrupted = 𝔼 X , X ~ ∼ C m ( ⋅ | X ) [ \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{corrupted}}=\mathbb{E}_{X,\tilde{X}\sim C_{m}(\cdot|X)}[ 𝔼 q ϕ ​ ( Z | X ~ ) ​ [ − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X | Z ) ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(Z|\tilde{X})}[-\log p_{\theta}(X|Z)] (11) + β ⋅ KL ( q ϕ ( Z | X ~ ) ∥ p ( Z ) ) ] . \displaystyle+\beta\cdot\mathrm{KL}(q_{\phi}(Z|\tilde{X})\|p(Z))]. The key difference is this information asymmetry: the encoder only gets partial information X ~ \tilde{X} , while the decoder has to predict everything, including what was masked. This forces Z Z to actually encode useful information from X ~ \tilde{X} —otherwise the decoder has no way to reconstruct the missing parts. A.2.2 Why Collapsed Solutions Become Suboptimal Consider what happens when the posterior collapses: q ϕ ​ ( Z | X ~ ) = p ⁡ ( Z ) q_{\phi}(Z|\tilde{X})=p(Z) . Now Z Z is independent of both X ~ \tilde{X} and X X , so: 𝔼 q ϕ ​ ( Z | X ~ ) = p ⁡ ( Z ) ​ [ − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X | Z ) ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(Z|\tilde{X})=p(Z)}[-\log p_{\theta}(X|Z)] = 𝔼 Z ∼ p ⁡ ( Z ) ​ [ − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X | Z ) ] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim p(Z)}[-\log p_{\theta}(X|Z)] (12) = 𝔼 Z ∼ p ⁡ ( Z ) ​ [ − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X ) ] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim p(Z)}[-\log p_{\theta}(X)] = − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X ) , \displaystyle=-\log p_{\theta}(X), where p θ ​ ( X ) p_{\theta}(X) is just the unconditional image distribution. We can break this down by what’s visible versus what’s masked: − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X ) = − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X visible ) − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X masked ) . -\log p_{\theta}(X)=-\log p_{\theta}(X_{\text{visible}})-\log p_{\theta}(X_{\text{masked}}). (13) The problem is the second term: − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X masked ) -\log p_{\theta}(X_{\text{masked}}) . Without any context, the decoder has to guess what’s in the masked regions based purely on dataset statistics—maybe “skies are usually blue” or “grass is usually green.” But this fails for any specific image. As we mask more pixels (higher m m ), this blind guessing gets worse and − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X ) -\log p_{\theta}(X) shoots up. Compare this to when Z Z actually encodes information from X ~ \tilde{X} . Now the decoder can use contextual clues—if it sees grass and trees in the visible parts, it knows this is probably an outdoor scene; if the visible colors are warm, maybe it’s sunset. This capability of recovering latent details from partial or degraded visual cues shares underlying principles with robust image processing pipelines designed for severely suboptimal conditions. This gives much better predictions: − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X | Z ) = − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X visible | Z ) − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X masked | Z ) , -\log p_{\theta}(X|Z)=-\log p_{\theta}(X_{\text{visible}}|Z)-\log p_{\theta}(X_{\text{masked}}|Z), (14) where − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X masked | Z ) -\log p_{\theta}(X_{\text{masked}}|Z) is now significantly smaller because the decoder can make informed guesses based on what Z Z encoded. Let’s define the benefit of having an informative Z Z as: Δ ≜ − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X ) − 𝔼 q ϕ ​ ( Z | X ~ ) ​ [ − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X | Z ) ] . \Delta\triangleq-\log p_{\theta}(X)-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(Z|\tilde{X})}[-\log p_{\theta}(X|Z)]. (15) Larger Δ \Delta means Z Z is more useful. Now compare total losses: Loss collapse \displaystyle\text{Loss}_{\text{collapse}} = − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X ) , \displaystyle=-\log p_{\theta}(X), (16) Loss informative \displaystyle\text{Loss}_{\text{informative}} = 𝔼 q ϕ ​ ( Z | X ~ ) ​ [ − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X | Z ) ] + β ⋅ ϵ , \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(Z|\tilde{X})}[-\log p_{\theta}(X|Z)]+\beta\cdot\epsilon, (17) where ϵ = KL ( q ϕ ( Z | X ~ ) ∥ p ( Z ) ) > 0 \epsilon=\mathrm{KL}(q_{\phi}(Z|\tilde{X})\|p(Z))>0 is the KL cost of keeping Z Z informative. The informative solution wins when: Δ > β ⋅ ϵ . \Delta>\beta\cdot\epsilon. (18) So the collapsed solution is suboptimal whenever β < Δ / ϵ \beta<\Delta/\epsilon . Here’s where masking matters: it directly increases Δ \Delta . As we mask more: • Without context (collapsed case), predicting more masked pixels becomes exponentially harder, pushing − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X ) -\log p_{\theta}(X) way up. • With context from Z Z (informative case), we can still make reasonable predictions based on visible cues, so 𝔼 ⁡ [ − log ⁡ p θ ​ ( X | Z ) ] \mathbb{E}[-\log p_{\theta}(X|Z)] stays relatively controlled. Higher m m widens the gap Δ \Delta , which means informative posteriors stay optimal for a broader range of β \beta (Eq. 18 ). Without masking, there’s a loophole: the decoder can just copy local patterns from the input. Even if Z Z is mostly useless, reconstructions still look okay, so Δ \Delta stays small and collapse becomes competitive. Masking closes this loophole—the decoder has to use Z Z to fill in the missing parts, which keeps information flowing through the latent space even under strong regularization. In conclusion, masking prevents collapse through a simple mechanism. First, it makes the reconstruction task harder, so Z Z needs to be informative. Second, if Z Z collapses and becomes useless, the decoder is forced to blindly guess large portions of the image, incurring huge losses. Third, by increasing Δ \Delta , masking ensures that keeping Z Z informative remains the better strategy across a wide range of β \beta values. This is how MacTok maintains meaningful continuous tokens even with aggressive compression and regularization.
